text.p: Semiconductor testing and assembly group Rood Technology NV said on Tuesday it was seeking a partnership with a major chips assembler.
"We are in talks with a number of parties," chairman Leo van Bree told a news conference on Rood's annual report, adding he hoped to reach an agreement this year.
Van Bree said he did not rule out Rood losing its independence by teaming up with another group.
But the conclusion that a bid for Rood's outstanding shares was pending would be "premature", he added.
Another major reshuffle of the company's business might take place in Southeast-Asia, where Rood has minority shares in three joint ventures with Singapore's Sunright Ltd.
Van Bree said Rood would "re-evaluate" its position in the joint operations in Singapore, Taiwan and Malaysia, as Sunright had not given voting rights that were previously promised.

Sunright planned to invest rather heavily in the joint ventures but Rood was in favour of more moderate investment schemes there, Van Bree said. He added that all options were still open, varying from selling Rood's interests to raising its stakes to levels with sufficient voting power.
Last year, the Asian joint ventures brought in a disappointing profit contribution of 0.4 million guilders, compared with 1.7 million in 1995.
Rood is also unhappy with the heavy capital requirements of the joint ventures in Asia, where Taiwanese banks in particular demand substantial guarantees.
This had already locked up some eight million guilders of Rood's funds, financial director Bart Brouwer said.
"The requests for financing the joint ventures for further investments are significant and further shareholders' support will be needed," Rood said in its annual report.
Rood earlier said it expected 1997 profits to recover from the disappointing results posted last year, but Van Bree declined to mention figures or percentages.
In 1996, the company's net profit almost dried up to 162,000 guilders, sharply down from 3.7 million in the previous year.
Van Bree said that although he was dissatisfied with 1996's profit figures, they were relatively favourable compared with general market trends.
After three years in which the semiconductors markets grew by 20 to 40 percent, the total market value suddenly fell by eight percent in 1996.
Volumes were still rising last year, but overcapacity in mainly memory chips put substantial pressure on prices.
Although this price pressure is not over yet, the markets are expected to recover in 1997 and the years ahead.
The personal computers and communications sectors are seen continuing their strong expansion and the demand for semiconductors will follow.
For the period 1996-2001 Rood expects an average value growth of its markets of about 16 percent per year, Van Bree said.
-- Theo Kolker, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
